item.title: China October 2026 CPI +0.7% y/y (expected +0.8%, prior +0.9%)
item.description:
A hot PPI and a soft CPI is a poor mix for China’s growth outlook. It points to margin compression for manufacturers and weak domestic demand, which weighs on sentiment toward Chinese equities and keeps expectations of policy support alive. For the yuan, softer underlying inflation argues for easier policy at the margin, a mild negative. For the Australian dollar and commodity currencies, the read is mixed: firm producer prices reflect cost pressure rather than a demand-led recovery in China’s appetite for raw materials. For oil, the PPI surge mainly shows the energy shock feeding through, not new demand strength.

---

Earlier:

  • China steps up market stabilisation push: three short-term priorities for equities

---

China’s factories are facing their fastest price rises in years while consumer inflation slips further below 1%, a split that points to squeezed margins and fragile domestic demand rather than any healthy reflation.

Summary:

  • China’s October PPI rose 5.7% y/y, beating the 5.3% forecast and up from 5% in September.
  • CPI rose 0.7% y/y, below the 0.8% expected and down from 0.9%.
  • CPI was flat month-on-month, in line with forecasts, after a 0.2% rise in September.
  • Core CPI eased to 0.8% from 1%, below the 0.9% forecast.
  • The gap between producer and consumer inflation has widened to around five percentage points.
  • Trade data is due Tuesday, with credit and money supply figures later in the week.

China’s factory-gate inflation accelerated more sharply than expected in October, while consumer price growth slowed below forecasts. The result widens the gap between surging producer costs and weak household demand.

The producer price index rose 5.7% from a year earlier, well above expectations of around 5.3% and up from 5% in September, when it had already reached a four-year high. Consumer prices increased 0.7% year-on-year, slightly below the 0.8% forecast and down from 0.9% in September. They were flat on the month, in line with expectations, after a 0.2% gain in September. Core inflation, which excludes food and energy, eased to 0.8% from 1%, also undershooting forecasts of 0.9%.

The divergence between the two measures has now widened to around five percentage points. Producer prices are being driven higher by energy and other input costs, while consumer prices show little sign of following. That suggests manufacturers and retailers are absorbing much of the cost increase rather than passing it on, a reflection of soft domestic demand and limited pricing power.

The core reading is the more telling figure for the health of the domestic economy. A slowdown in underlying inflation to below 1% points to subdued demand for services and non-essential goods, despite some support from spending around the National Day Golden Week holiday at the start of October.

For policymakers, the mix is awkward. Weak consumer and core inflation strengthens the case for further support for domestic demand. The jump in producer prices, though, limits room for aggressive easing and squeezes industrial profit margins at a time when firms are already facing higher energy costs linked to the war with Iran.

The data come as Beijing is also moving to shore up confidence in its stock market, with a recent State Council meeting calling for stronger capital market stabilisation mechanisms.

Attention now turns to October trade data due on Tuesday, which will show whether export strength can continue to offset sluggish domestic demand. Credit and money supply figures follow later in the week.

---

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: ICYMI: Goldman cuts gold forecasts to $4,150 for 2026, $4,800 for 2027 as hawkish Fed bites
item.description:
Goldman’s cut adds weight to the view that rates, not geopolitics, are setting gold’s direction for now. With December Fed hike odds near 80%, that keeps a lid on near-term rallies. The bank’s warning that higher oil prices could trigger systematic selling fits the way gold has traded through the Iran war: escalation lifts crude and yields, which weighs on bullion. Weekend strikes in Iraq and Saudi Arabia raise that risk this week. The heavy central bank bid underpins the longer-term case and is likely to cushion deeper dips. A shift toward Fed easing in late 2027 is the bank’s main upside catalyst.

---

Earlier:

  • Gold ticks higher on softer oil, but Fed’s 80% December hike odds cap gain

---

Goldman has lowered its gold targets as Fed hikes erode hedging demand, but it is betting that relentless central bank buying will still carry bullion higher by the end of 2027.

Summary:

  • Goldman cut its end-2026 gold target to $4,150 an ounce from $4,650, and its end-2027 target to $4,800 from $5,400.
  • The bank cites a hawkish Fed, including an expected December hike, curbing demand for gold as a policy hedge.
  • Central banks are expected to buy around 60 tonnes a month in 2026 and 2027. Current buying is estimated at around 85 tonnes.
  • Central bank demand drives most of the roughly 15% upside Goldman forecasts by end-2027.
  • A more hawkish Fed path could leave gold near $4,660 by end-2027, while fiscal worries could push it above the base case.
  • Fed rate cuts, expected from late 2027, are seen as a further source of support.

Goldman Sachs has cut its gold price forecasts, lowering its end-2026 target to $4,150 an ounce from $4,650 and its end-2027 target to $4,800 from $5,400, as an increasingly hawkish Federal Reserve weighs on investor demand for the metal.

The bank’s strategists, in a note dated November 5, said the revisions assume the Fed’s tighter stance, including an expected rate hike in December, will limit demand for gold as a hedge against currency debasement and wider policy risk. They expect that hedging demand to drift back toward historical averages rather than return to the elevated levels seen earlier this year, and they see interest in gold call options moderating as well.

Goldman compared the current backdrop with 2022, when heavy central bank buying underpinned prices but rising interest rates held back investment demand. Higher rates make interest-bearing assets more competitive with gold, which offers no yield.

Even so, the bank kept a constructive longer-term view, anchored by official-sector demand. It expects central banks to buy around 60 tonnes a month through 2026 and 2027, well above the pre-2022 average of 17 tonnes. It estimates current purchases at roughly 85 tonnes a month on a seasonally adjusted three-month basis. That buying drives most of the roughly 15% upside Goldman forecasts by the end of 2027. The strategists noted that emerging-market central banks, particularly China, still hold relatively small gold allocations compared with potential long-term targets. They also said the debate is increasingly shifting from whether to own gold to where to store it, reflecting concerns over reserve security and trust between countries.

Goldman expects further support once the Fed begins cutting rates, which its economists see starting in late 2027 and continuing into early 2028. In the nearer term, however, the bank sees headwinds over the next three to six months for commodity trading advisers and macro hedge funds, from rising rates, uncertain energy prices and tighter risk limits. It warned that higher oil prices could prompt further selling by systematic strategies.

On the risks, Goldman said a further Fed hike in March 2027, delayed easing or a higher projected terminal rate could leave gold at around $4,660 by end-2027, below its base case. Renewed worries over government debt sustainability, by contrast, could lift prices above its central forecast.

The cut follows a sharp reversal for bullion. Gold gained around 64% in 2025, its best year since 1979, and peaked near $5,600 in January before falling to around $4,070 by November 6, nearly 27% below that high. Goldman said longer-term investors seeking exposure to central bank buying or protection against policy risk may see the correction as a potential entry point.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Gold ticks higher on softer oil, but Fed’s 80% December hike odds cap gain
item.description:
In this war, gold trades through the oil, inflation and rates channel rather than as a safe haven. That makes crude the key cross-asset signal: softer oil helps bullion, and renewed escalation hurts it. Weekend developments (Rubio’s downbeat take on talks, the Khor Mor and Riyadh strikes, Hormuz disruptions) leave that support vulnerable if oil reprices higher. US CPI this week is the next test for December hike pricing, and therefore for gold’s opportunity cost. Physical and official-sector buying should help limit dips, but they’re unlikely to offset a further hawkish shift in rates on their own.

Gold is being pulled between softer oil and bargain-hunting on one side and a hawkish Fed and global tightening on the other, with the Iran war acting through oil prices rather than as a safe-haven bid.

Summary:

  • Gold edged higher in Asia on Monday after a weekly gain of roughly 5%.
  • Softer oil, after Trump played down new strikes on Iran, eased inflation concerns.
  • Weekend escalation, including Rubio’s comments and strikes in Iraq and Saudi Arabia, leaves oil, and therefore gold, exposed.
  • Strong US payrolls and 4.1% unemployment lifted December Fed hike odds to around 80%, from about 70%.
  • A former BOJ chief economist expects a December BOJ hike, adding to global tightening.
  • Indian festival demand and central bank buying offer support, while a firm dollar remains a constraint.

Gold edged higher in Asian trade on Monday, building on a weekly gain of roughly 5%, as softer oil prices eased some of the inflation concerns that have weighed on bullion. Gains were kept in check, however, by firming expectations that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates again in December after a robust US jobs report.

The relationship between gold and the Iran war has run counter to the traditional safe-haven script. Rather than rallying on escalation, bullion has tended to fall when geopolitical risk rises, because higher oil prices lift inflation expectations, push up bond yields and strengthen the case for tighter Fed policy. Monday’s modest bounce fits that pattern. Oil fell after President Donald Trump said he was highly unlikely to order fresh strikes on Iran as long as talks continued, giving gold some breathing room.

That support looks fragile. Over the weekend, Secretary of State Marco Rubio described talks with Tehran as not productive, a suspected Iranian drone strike halted output at a major Iraqi gas field, and Houthi forces hit targets in Riyadh including the Aramco Tower. Washington and Tehran also both reported shipping disruptions near the Strait of Hormuz. If those developments push oil higher again, the inflation and rates channel would likely turn back against gold.

The Fed remains the biggest headwind. US job growth accelerated in October and the unemployment rate fell to 4.1%, reinforcing the view that the labour market is resilient. Traders now see around an 80% chance of a December rate hike, up from about 70% before the payrolls release, according to CME’s FedWatch tool. Higher rates raise the opportunity cost of holding a non-yielding asset such as gold. The data also revived hike expectations that had faded somewhat during the post-election equity selloff and amid concerns that weaker AI-driven demand could slow the economy.

The tightening trend extends beyond the US. A former Bank of Japan chief economist expects the BOJ to raise rates in December and keep lifting borrowing costs toward 2% next year, adding to a global backdrop of higher yields that tends to weigh on bullion.

There are offsetting sources of support. Physical demand in India picked up at the start of a key festival on Friday, as lower prices drew back bargain hunters who had held off for months waiting for a correction. Central bank buying has also been a steady structural pillar for gold in recent years, as reserve managers diversify away from the US dollar, and that demand has tended to absorb price dips. Any renewed stress in risk assets, including AI-related equities, could also revive interest in gold as a portfolio diversifier.

Against that, a firm US dollar, supported by wide rate differentials, remains a constraint, and investment flows have been sensitive to shifts in Fed expectations.

The balance for gold this week is likely to hinge on oil and US inflation data, with Tuesday’s CPI release a key test of how far the Fed’s hiking case has to run.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Markets price three more BoE hikes, but analysts see a shallower path after move to 4%
item.description:
The gap between futures pricing and analyst expectations is the key tension for UK assets. If the BoE delivers only one more hike, front-end gilt yields have room to fall and the curve could rally, which is why several analysts favour adding duration. For sterling, a shallower path than priced is a mild headwind on rate differentials. Analysts see little chance of the BoE out-tightening its peers, which limits the pound’s upside. Oil is the swing factor: a sustained rise on Iran escalation, as this weekend’s headlines threaten, would push the BoE back toward the market’s hawkish pricing.

---

  • investingLive European news wrap: BoE raises bank rate to 4.00% as expected

---

The BoE has bought insurance against an energy-driven inflation spiral, but analysts broadly think markets are overpaying for further protection, with one more hike looking more likely than three.

Summary:

  • The BoE raised Bank Rate by 25bp to 4% in a unanimous vote, with inflation at 3.5% and rising.
  • Markets price three more hikes by the end of next year, more than most economists expect.
  • Many analysts see the move as a risk-management hike aimed at preventing second-round effects from the energy shock.
  • One further hike, most likely in February, is the common base case, though some see the move as “one and done” if energy prices ease.
  • Inflation is seen peaking at around 4.5% next summer, with the Iran war and oil prices the key risk.
  • Several analysts see value in gilts, particularly the seven- to eight-year area.

Markets are pricing three more Bank of England rate hikes by the end of next year, but analysts reacting to last week’s move increasingly doubt the central bank will need to go that far. Most see one further increase as the more likely path.

The BoE raised Bank Rate by 25 basis points to 4% in a unanimous decision, aiming to contain inflation that is running at 3.5% and still rising. The move was widely expected and caused little disruption in markets, but analysts said the unanimity could reinforce expectations of further tightening.

The driver is the energy shock from the war with Iran. Policymakers are concerned that higher energy costs will pass through to consumers and become embedded in the economy, and they are using higher borrowing costs to cool demand. One forecast sees inflation peaking later and higher than previously thought, at around 4.5% next summer, as energy prices continue to grind higher. The key question, analysts said, is whether this imported shock stays contained or spills into domestic wages and services prices.

Several analysts characterised the decision as a risk-management or insurance hike rather than the start of an aggressive cycle. In this view, the Bank is acting to protect its credibility and limit second-round effects, even though evidence of energy costs becoming embedded in wider wages and prices remains limited. Resilient growth, consumer spending and labour market data have given it both a reason to hike and the room to do so.

That has opened a gap between market pricing and economists’ expectations. Futures imply significantly more tightening than most forecasters anticipate. Higher bond yields are already doing some of the Bank’s work, and higher energy bills, mortgage rates and tighter financial conditions are expected to weigh on household spending. One analyst said the move could prove “one and done” if energy prices ease before February, while others see one further hike, most likely in February, as the base case.

The outlook remains closely tied to the Middle East. A prolonged conflict that keeps oil prices elevated into 2027 would strengthen the case for further tightening. Analysts flagged a return to US strikes on Iran, or rising domestic political uncertainty, as risks to a shallower path.

For investors, a number of analysts see value in gilts after the rise in yields. Some favour the seven- to eight-year part of the curve and gradually extending duration, arguing that much of the UK’s fiscal and supply risk is already priced. For sterling, the key issue is whether the BoE ends up tightening much more than other major central banks, which analysts view as unlikely for now. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6799 – Reuters estimate
item.description:
Earlier:

  • China steps up market stabilisation push: three short-term priorities for equities
The People’s Bank of China is due to set the daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 0115 GMT (2115 US Eastern time), a fixing that remains one of the most closely watched signals in Asian foreign exchange markets. China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, under which the renminbi (yuan) is allowed to trade within a prescribed band around a central reference rate, or midpoint, set each trading day by the PBOC. The current trading band permits the currency to move plus or minus 2% from the official midpoint during onshore trading hours. Each morning, the PBOC determines the midpoint based on a range of inputs. These include the previous day’s closing price, movements in major currencies, particularly the US dollar, broader international FX conditions, and domestic economic considerations such as capital flows, growth momentum and financial stability objectives. The midpoint is not a purely mechanical calculation, allowing policymakers discretion to guide market expectations. Once the midpoint is announced, onshore USD/CNY is free to trade within the allowable band. If market pressures push the yuan toward either edge of that range, the central bank may step in to smooth volatility. Intervention can take the form of direct buying or selling of yuan, adjustments to liquidity conditions, or guidance through state-owned banks. As a result, the daily fixing is often interpreted as a policy signal rather than just a technical reference point. A stronger-than-expected CNY midpoint is typically read as a sign the PBOC is leaning against depreciation pressure, while a weaker fixing for the CNY can indicate tolerance for a softer currency, often in response to dollar strength or domestic economic headwinds.In periods of heightened global volatility, such as shifts in US rate expectations, trade tensions or capital flow pressures, the fixing takes on added significance. For investors, it provides insight into Beijing’s currency priorities, balancing competitiveness, capital stability and financial market confidence.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Trump eyes Xi, Putin meeting at APEC on Iran war, says he’d ‘certainly take’ Huang
item.description:
For oil, a Trump, Xi and Putin meeting focused partly on ending the Iran war is a potential de-escalation catalyst. It sits awkwardly with Rubio’s assessment that talks with Tehran are not productive and with the weekend’s strikes on regional energy infrastructure, so crude is likely to treat it as a headline to watch rather than a reason to reprice. For Nvidia, Trump’s backing offers some cushion ahead of tonight’s first session since Huang’s admission, though his “you never know” caveat stops short of a full endorsement. Whether Huang is on the trip will be read as a signal of his standing on China chip policy.

---

Trump is heading to China with Iran and nuclear arms on the agenda for possible talks with Xi and Putin, and he says he would gladly bring Jensen Huang along, a show of support that could become a test of Huang’s political standing.

Summary:

  • Trump said he thinks he will meet Xi and Putin at next week’s APEC summit in China.
  • Talks would cover a lot of ground, including denuclearisation and ending the war in Iran.
  • He said he had not spoken to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang about the allegations, but called him a fine, honorable person.
  • Trump said Huang probably had an explanation that should be heard, and that he would certainly take him on the Asia trip.
  • Trump said he was “only kidding” about naming UFC chief Dana White as White House press secretary.

US President Donald Trump said he expects to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin at next week’s APEC summit in China. He also said he would be willing to take Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang on the trip, despite the controversy over Huang’s relationship with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset.

Speaking to reporters on Sunday, Trump said a meeting with Xi and Putin “will be interesting” and would cover a lot of ground, including denuclearisation and ending the war in Iran, Reuters reported. Such a meeting would bring the leaders of the US, China and Russia together as the Iran conflict grinds through its eighth month.

On Huang, Trump said he had not spoken to the Nvidia chief about the allegations but described him as a fine and honourable person who had done an amazing job for the United States. He added that Huang probably had an explanation and that it should be heard, while acknowledging that “you never know what is going on.” Asked whether Huang would join him in Asia, Trump said he did not know but would certainly take him.

Trump’s remarks came on the same day that Huang admitted to a romantic relationship with Alice Huang, a Megaspeed executive whom US officials reportedly believe was recruited by Chinese intelligence, and that Nvidia’s board opened an independent investigation. The board has said it has no reason to believe national security or company secrets were compromised, and Huang remains chief executive.

Whether Huang travels to China alongside the president will be closely watched. His presence would signal that the White House still sees him as a key voice on AI and chip policy. His absence would suggest the affair has begun to cost him political access at a sensitive moment for US export controls.

In a lighter moment, Trump said he had only been kidding about naming Ultimate Fighting Championship chief executive Dana White as White House press secretary. He said White loved the idea and that the two would speak on Monday about other matters.

For markets, the APEC summit now looms as a significant event, with any progress on Iran carrying implications for oil and any signal on chips bearing directly on Nvidia. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Recap - BOJ’s Ueda sees inflation near 2% but flags upside risks as energy costs bite
item.description:
Ueda’s acknowledgement of upside inflation risks, with energy costs set to push price growth higher into early next year, leans hawkish. It supports expectations that the BOJ will keep normalising policy, which is mildly supportive for the yen and keeps upward pressure on Japanese government bond yields. His comment that the BOJ watches other central banks closely, including their effect on exchange rates, keeps yen moves on the policy radar. Georgieva’s warning on AI-related volatility adds to a theme already weighing on global tech this week.

---Ueda is comfortable that Japan has reached 2% underlying inflation, but with energy costs feeding through and upside risks building, the BOJ’s job has shifted from getting there to holding the line.

Summary:

  • Ueda said the BOJ expects underlying inflation to stay around 2% but sees some upside risks.
  • Energy-related price rises are feeding into consumer inflation, with price growth seen accelerating into early next year.
  • Wages are growing at a pace consistent with 2% inflation, though the target has yet to become a social norm.
  • The BOJ is watching other central banks closely, given their impact on exchange rates and interest rates.
  • Unconventional tools could be used again if a severe shock hit, with care taken to limit side effects.
  • IMF chief Georgieva said AI-related market volatility would complicate central banks’ work.

I was away from the desk on Friday, so I’m catching up on a few items worth revisiting. First up are comments from Bank of Japan Governor Kazuo Ueda, who said the central bank expects underlying inflation to stay around its 2% target but sees some upside risks.

Speaking at a seminar hosted by the International Monetary Fund in Washington, Ueda said higher energy-related prices were starting to feed into consumer inflation and that price growth was likely to accelerate further into early next year, Reuters reported. He described Japan as being in an equilibrium in which wages are growing at a pace consistent with 2% inflation.

Even so, Ueda said the 2% target had yet to become a social norm in Japan, and that the BOJ’s goal now is to anchor underlying inflation around that level. Having reached it, the task is to keep it there.

He said the BOJ watches the actions of other central banks very closely because they influence asset prices, including exchange rates and interest rates, and reveal how policymakers elsewhere view their own economies. On unconventional tools, he said they had some positive effects when used but were not perfect substitutes for cutting rates from positive levels. The BOJ may have to use them again depending on the severity of any future shock. In that case, he said, it should look to limit side effects, including on market functioning.

Asked about the debate over central bank communication prompted by new Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh, Ueda said a balance was needed between explaining policy goals and avoiding moral hazard in markets.

On artificial intelligence, Ueda said rapid advances had delivered a positive demand shock to Japan’s economy, while supply-side effects still needed study. He suggested that Japan, with its severe labour shortages, could benefit more than some countries from AI replacing labour. He also flagged concern about cyber risks to financial stability, saying some small banks and firms had not done enough to protect themselves.

IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva, speaking at the same event, noted recent weakness in AI-related stocks and said central bankers would need to weigh any slowdown in AI-driven growth. She warned that concerns over dependence on the AI investment boom and high valuations were affecting markets globally. The resulting volatility, she said, would complicate central banks’ work at a time of rising risks to price stability.

For markets, the takeaway is a BOJ governor who sees inflation risks tilted higher, keeping the focus on the bank’s next policy steps and the yen.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: China steps up market stabilisation push: three short-term priorities for equities
item.description:
The State Council’s call reinforces the sense of a policy floor under Chinese equities. That should help cap downside volatility in mainland and Hong Kong shares, particularly at times of global risk aversion like the current AI-led wobble in tech. The emphasis is on execution rather than new stimulus, so the immediate upside impulse is likely limited. The market will want evidence of actual inflows and buyback activity before rewarding it. A steadier Chinese equity market is mildly supportive for the yuan and for China-sensitive currencies such as the Australian dollar.

---

---

Beijing is signalling that its stock market safety net is staying firmly in place, with the focus now on making existing support measures deliver real money into the market rather than announcing new ones.

Summary:

  • A recent State Council executive meeting called for improved capital market stabilisation mechanisms to enhance stock market stability.
  • An economist said the short-term priority is faster, fuller implementation of existing stabilisation policies.
  • Greater participation by financial institutions and listed companies is being urged, alongside tracking of real fund injections, buybacks and stake increases.
  • Authorities should dynamically monitor supply and demand for funds, to avoid concentrated short-term funding pressure and negative feedback.
  • Over the medium to long term, mechanisms for long-term capital to enter the market should be strengthened.

China is moving to strengthen the mechanisms it uses to steady its stock market, Securities Times reported. A recent State Council executive meeting called for an improved capital market stabilisation framework to enhance the market’s inherent stability and support its steady and healthy development.

The cabinet-level call signals that Beijing intends to keep a firm hand under equities, building on a series of support measures already rolled out. The focus now appears to be shifting from announcing new tools to making sure existing ones deliver.

A chief economist at a Chinese securities firm, quoted in the report, said the short-term priority should be faster and fuller implementation of the stabilisation policies already in place. That includes greater participation by financial institutions and listed companies. It also means closer tracking of how much money is actually being injected into the market, and of progress on share buybacks and stake increases by major shareholders, so that the measures have their full effect.

He also called for dynamic monitoring of shifts in the balance of supply and demand for funds in the market. The aim, he said, is to avoid a concentrated release of short-term funding pressure that could feed back negatively into market sentiment. That points to a concern that a cluster of new share supply could overwhelm buying at sensitive moments.

Over the medium to long term, the economist said China should keep improving the channels through which long-term capital enters the stock market, to make the market more stable and resilient over time.

For investors, the message is that the authorities remain focused on limiting downside volatility in Chinese equities, with the emphasis on execution and monitoring rather than fresh stimulus. The key markers to watch are further signs of policy follow-through, including disclosed buyback activity and inflows from state-linked and long-term investors.

---

Securities Times is a Chinese financial newspaper based in Shenzhen and published under the People’s Daily group. It is one of the outlets designated by China’s securities regulator for listed company disclosures and is widely read for official and market-related commentary on Chinese capital markets. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: China October inflation preview: CPI seen near 0.8%, PPI above 5%
item.description:
A PPI print above 5% alongside sub-1% CPI would reinforce the market’s read that China is importing cost pressure without the demand to pass it on. That is a negative mix for industrial profits and for confidence in the domestic recovery. A soft CPI reading would keep expectations alive for further policy support from Beijing, which would weigh modestly on the yuan. For commodity-linked currencies such as the Australian dollar, the key signal is demand: weak consumer prices argue against a strong pickup in China’s appetite for raw materials. For oil, firm PPI mainly reflects the energy shock already under way rather than new demand strength.

---

China’s October inflation data is expected to show factory-gate prices racing ahead while consumer prices barely move, a split that points to squeezed margins and fragile domestic demand rather than a healthy reflation.

Summary:

  • China’s October CPI and PPI are due at 01:30 GMT, 8:30pm US Eastern on Sunday.
  • CPI is forecast at around 0.8% y/y, down from 0.9%, with estimates clustered between 0.7% and 0.9%.
  • Core CPI is expected to hold near 1%.
  • PPI is forecast to rise to around 5.2% to 5.3% from 5%, extending a four-year high.
  • Monthly PPI gains are seen slowing sharply, but not enough to stop the annual rate climbing.
  • Trade data follows on 10 November, with credit and money supply figures on 13 November.

China releases October consumer and producer price data at 01:30 GMT on Monday, 8:30pm US Eastern time on Sunday. Forecasts point to a further widening of the gap between subdued consumer inflation and rapidly rising factory-gate prices.

Consumer prices are expected to rise around 0.8% from a year earlier, edging down from 0.9% in September. Forecasts are tightly clustered, with most estimates sitting between 0.7% and 0.9%. Some forecasters see prices unchanged on the month, after a 0.2% rise in September that undershot expectations. Core inflation, which strips out food and energy, is projected to hold near 1%.

Consumer demand has been subdued but steady. Spending ahead of the National Day Golden Week holiday in early October offered some support, although purchases brought forward before the break diluted its impact on the month as a whole.

The producer price index is where the pressure lies. Annual PPI inflation is forecast to rise to around 5.2% to 5.3%, with some estimates higher, from 5% in September, when it hit a four-year high and comfortably beat expectations. Energy costs have been a key driver of the acceleration. Month-on-month gains are expected to slow sharply from September’s pace, but not by enough to stop the annual rate from climbing further.

That combination is the central story. Rising producer prices alongside consumer inflation stuck below 1% suggest that manufacturers are absorbing much of the cost increase rather than passing it on to households, a sign of weak pricing power in a soft domestic economy. It also squeezes industrial profit margins.

The data open a busy week for China. October trade figures follow on 10 November, after exports surged in September. Money supply, new loans and total social financing are due on 13 November.

A CPI print at or below forecast would reinforce the picture of fragile domestic demand. A PPI surprise to the upside would add to concerns over imported cost pressure and keep the focus on how long China’s factories can hold the line on prices.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Blumenthal sets Jan 4 deadline for Binance, Tether and Trump crypto firms as power shifts

---

Blumenthal has spent most of a year writing letters to crypto firms; from January his requests come with the power to compel answers.

Summary:

  • In letters announced on November 5, Senator Richard Blumenthal renewed his records demands to Binance, Tether, World Liberty Financial and Fight Fight Fight LLC
  • World Liberty and Fight Fight Fight must start producing documents by November 30, and all four firms face a final deadline of January 4, 2027
  • January 4 is one day after the new Congress convenes, when Blumenthal is expected to chair the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations
  • As ranking member he can only request voluntary cooperation, and he has warned of further measures, widely read as subpoenas, if the firms don’t comply
  • The inquiries cover Iran-linked transfers at Binance, Tether’s payments to a firm linked to Bo Hines, and the Trump family’s crypto ventures
  • Bitcoin briefly fell below $76,000 on the election results before recovering, and ether hit a two-month low in the same move

US Senator Richard Blumenthal has given Binance, Tether and two crypto businesses tied to President Donald Trump until January 4, 2027, to hand over outstanding records, and the date matters more than the demand. It falls one day after the new Congress convenes, when Blumenthal is expected to take the chair of the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations following the Democrats’ sweep of both chambers in the November 3 midterms.

The letters, announced on November 5, went to Binance, Tether, World Liberty Financial and Fight Fight Fight LLC, the company behind the TRUMP memecoin. World Liberty and Fight Fight Fight were asked to begin producing documents by November 30. Blumenthal warned the subcommittee would look at other ways to secure compliance if the records were not delivered by the January deadline, and coverage of the Democratic sweep has read that as a signal subpoenas could follow. CNN reported that the same round of letters also went to Trump administration officials and several large corporate donors.

None of the underlying lines of inquiry is new. Blumenthal opened his investigation into World Liberty Financial and the TRUMP coin in May 2025. In February he pressed Binance over a reported $1.7 billion in Iran-linked transfers, which the exchange disputed, saying its sanctions-related exposure had fallen sharply since early 2024. In October he wrote to Tether over reported payments to a consulting firm co-founded by former White House crypto adviser Bo Hines, which Tether has said involved no wrongdoing, and to Cantor Fitzgerald over its ties to the stablecoin issuer.

What has changed is leverage. As the minority’s ranking member, Blumenthal could only ask for voluntary cooperation, and recipients are not obliged to respond until the new Congress is seated. From January, the requests come from a subcommittee chair with the tools to compel documents.

For Bitcoin and ether, the direct price impact looks limited for now. The market has already absorbed the larger political shock: Bitcoin briefly fell below $76,000 as results came in on November 4 before recovering, while ether dropped to a two-month low in the same move, according to market reports. The letters target named companies, not the assets themselves. The more plausible channel to prices runs through Washington’s calendar, where an investigations-heavy agenda could compete for time with the stalled CLARITY Act market structure bill. A longer wait for clear US rules would likely weigh on sentiment more than any single letter. Tether is the exception worth watching, because USDT is the largest stablecoin and a core source of trading liquidity, so sustained pressure on its compliance record would touch market plumbing in a way a probe of a memecoin promoter would not. Ether’s sharper election-week drop suggests it has been the more sensitive of the two to US policy risk, though that is an observation from one move rather than a fixed relationship.

What to watch next: the first marker is November 30, when World Liberty and Fight Fight Fight are due to start producing records, and a refusal or thin response would make January subpoenas more likely. The second is how quickly the subcommittee acts once Blumenthal holds the gavel. Readers should also track US spot Bitcoin and ether ETF flows against price over the period. Steady inflows with a stable price would suggest the market is treating the probe as headline risk, while falling prices despite inflows would point to selling pressure elsewhere. A subpoena aimed specifically at Tether would be the clearest reason to reassess, since it would move the investigation closer to market infrastructure. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Weekend: Houthis hit Riyadh’s Aramco Tower and target oil storage as Saudi supply risk grows
item.description:
This is an escalation risk for crude rather than a confirmed supply loss: Saudi Arabia reports minor damage and intercepted missiles, and no outage has been reported. What matters is the direction. Aramco storage is now being targeted, and the Houthis have a declared maritime embargo against Saudi Arabia, at a time when Hormuz flows are already disrupted and Saudi barrels routed via the Red Sea matter more for global supply. Coming on top of the suspected Iranian strike on Iraq’s Khor Mor gas field and Rubio’s warning that talks with Tehran are not productive, it strengthens the case for a firmer war-risk premium. Traders will be watching for any confirmed damage to Saudi output, storage or Red Sea loadings.

---

A Houthi strike on Riyadh’s financial district, with Aramco oil storage also in the crosshairs, shows the Iran war’s reach now extends deep into the world’s largest oil exporter, just as Saudi Red Sea exports matter most.

Summary:

  • Houthi forces struck the Aramco Tower in Riyadh’s financial district on Saturday.
  • The group said it also targeted Riyadh’s airport and Aramco oil storage facilities. Saudi Arabia said several missiles were intercepted and destroyed.
  • Saudi Arabia’s energy ministry reported minor damage and no casualties, though verified footage suggests heavier damage to at least one floor.
  • The strike followed Houthi claims that a Saudi-led coalition air strike killed at least 33 people in Yemen.
  • The Houthis have declared a maritime embargo on Saudi Arabia and have attacked oil facilities and Red Sea tankers since a ceasefire collapsed in July.

Yemen’s Houthi movement has struck the Aramco Tower in the heart of Riyadh’s financial district and claimed separate attacks on the Saudi capital’s airport and Aramco oil storage facilities. The strikes underline how the Iran war is increasingly putting the world’s largest oil exporter in the firing line.

The Saudi energy ministry said the skyscraper suffered only minor damage and that no one was killed or injured. However, footage verified by the BBC suggests the damage was more extensive, with at least one floor appearing badly hit by a missile or drone and windows shattered across more than one level. Saudi Arabia said its air defences intercepted and destroyed several missiles.

A statement carried by the Houthi-run Saba news agency confirmed the group had targeted Riyadh’s business district on Saturday, without naming the tower. The strikes are the latest in a series against targets deep inside Saudi Arabia that the kingdom has struggled to contain in recent months.

The attack followed Houthi accusations that a Saudi-led coalition air strike had killed at least 33 people, including women and children, in a town east of Sanaa. Saudi Arabia has not commented on that claim.

For oil markets, the targeting of Aramco storage is the key development. The Tehran-backed group has already declared what it calls a maritime embargo against Saudi Arabia. It has attacked airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea since an informal ceasefire collapsed in July. With shipping through the Strait of Hormuz still disrupted, Saudi export routes via the Red Sea have taken on added importance, which makes any threat to them more significant for global supply.

The conflict in Yemen, largely dormant for several years, has flared again since the Iran war began, with major fighting resuming between Houthi forces and troops aligned with the Saudi-backed government.

Taken together with a suspected Iranian drone strike on an Iraqi gas field and a harder US line on stalled talks with Tehran, the Riyadh attack adds to signs that the regional conflict is widening rather than winding down. The next test is whether strikes on Saudi energy infrastructure cause any measurable disruption to output or exports.  

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: RBA’s Hunter warns AI could trigger sharp asset repricing as boom adds to inflation
item.description:
Hunter’s description of AI as a near-term inflationary force supports the RBA’s tightening bias rather than pointing to relief. That underpins the Australian dollar on rate differentials and keeps the focus on the risk of further hikes. Her financial stability warning adds a central bank voice to growing market unease over AI valuations and funding, at a time when tech-linked assets are already under strain. Any further move toward repricing would favour defensive positioning in AI-exposed equities. It could also limit the Australian dollar’s upside if global risk sentiment sours.

---

Last week:

  • investingLive Asia-Pacific market news: RBA hikes to 18-year high

---

The RBA sees AI as an inflation problem today and a potential financial stability problem tomorrow, with little sign yet of the productivity payoff that would justify the investment boom.

Summary:

  • RBA Assistant Governor Sarah Hunter said AI may be increasing risks to financial stability.
  • Some asset prices could face sharp repricing, or disorderly adjustments, if returns on AI investment disappoint.
  • There is limited evidence AI has materially lifted aggregate productivity or had large effects on employment in advanced economies.
  • In the near term, AI-driven demand against constrained supply adds upward pressure on inflation. The long-run effect is likely broadly neutral.
  • There are tentative signs of labour market adjustment in AI-exposed occupations, particularly for younger workers.
  • The data centre boom is one reason the RBA has hiked five times this year, to 4.85%.

Reserve Bank of Australia Assistant Governor Sarah Hunter has warned that artificial intelligence could pose growing risks to financial stability. She said some asset prices would be exposed to sharp repricing, or even disorderly adjustments, if returns on AI investment fall short of expectations.

Speaking at a UBS conference in Sydney on Monday, Hunter said there was limited evidence so far that AI had materially lifted aggregate productivity, and little sign it had caused large effects on employment across advanced economies, according to Reuters.

On inflation, her view was that AI’s impact would change over time. In the near term, she said, the technology acts as a positive shock to demand at a time when the economy’s supply capacity is constrained, which adds upward pressure on prices. Over the longer run, she expects supply to catch up as data centre capacity and related industries expand, easing bottlenecks. If AI then delivers broader productivity gains, the initial inflationary pressure from the investment boom is likely to fade, leaving the long-run effect broadly neutral.

The comments carry weight for the policy outlook. A surge in domestic data centre investment has been one of the forces adding to demand in the Australian economy. It is among the reasons the RBA has raised its cash rate five times this year, taking it to an 18-year high of 4.85%. Hunter’s description of AI as a near-term inflationary force fits with that tightening rather than pointing to any early relief.

Hunter also noted tentative signs of adjustment in the labour market. Job advertisements and employment outcomes have been weaker in occupations more exposed to AI, while growth has been stronger in areas where the technology has had less impact, particularly for younger workers.

Her financial stability warning lands at a sensitive moment for global markets, with investors already scrutinising the scale of AI spending and the debt and long-term commitments being taken on to fund it. Hunter stopped short of predicting a correction, framing the risk as conditional on investment returns disappointing.

For traders, the takeaway is a central bank that sees AI adding to inflation now while keeping an eye on the risk of a sharp reversal in the asset prices tied to it. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Is NVDA stock a buy or sell? Spy alert?
item.description:
Nvidia stock: Sell, hold or trim after spy allegations? Why $181, $172 and $164 matter

Nvidia's board has opened an investigation into reports involving CEO Jensen Huang and alleged Chinese espionage. For shareholders facing another potentially volatile week, the important questions are what has actually been established, whether the investment case has changed, and what the stock price reveals next.

November 8, 2026 | NVDA price analysis based on the November 6 regular-session close of $186.64.

Nvidia (NVDA) shareholders face an uncomfortable combination of sensational headlines, unresolved national-security allegations and an already weakened stock price. But a board investigation is not proof of espionage, and a sharp selloff does not automatically mean investors should sell. The levels around $181, $172 and $164 offer a practical framework for assessing what happens next.

For a closer look at the potential fallout for Nvidia and its shareholders, read our analysis of three risks facing Nvidia shares following Jensen Huang's admission and the reported Chinese espionage allegations.

Nvidia shareholders: The quick decision map

Watch levels, not predictions. The purpose of this map is to help investors evaluate new evidence, not tell every shareholder to make the same decision.

What do we actually know about the Nvidia spy allegations?

The story is serious enough to deserve attention, but not every circulating claim deserves equal credibility.

On Sunday, November 8, Nvidia announced that its board was initiating an independent investigation following reports that CEO Jensen Huang had been targeted by a foreign intelligence operation.

Independent directors and outside legal counsel will oversee the inquiry. The board said it currently has no reason to believe company secrets or US national-security interests were compromised. It also expressed confidence in Huang's leadership.

That is a meaningful statement from the company, although it is not a completed investigation or independent finding of innocence.

What about Huang's reported personal relationship?

According to Reuters, Huang acknowledged in a message to employees that he had been unfaithful to his wife, apologized and accepted responsibility for his conduct.

The reports concern Alice Huang, a former executive associated with Singapore-based Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer. US intelligence reportedly suspects she was involved in efforts to obtain information for Chinese intelligence.

However, an admission of infidelity does not establish that Jensen Huang knowingly assisted an intelligence operation, disclosed confidential information or violated the law.

There is also important contradictory information.

Singapore's Ministry of Home Affairs said on October 31 that its authorities had not investigated Alice Huang over the reported intelligence allegations. Investigations involving Megaspeed itself remain ongoing.

Meanwhile, senior US lawmakers have requested a closed-door congressional briefing from Jensen Huang, reflecting the seriousness with which some officials are treating the reporting. The requested briefing is not proof of wrongdoing.

What matters financially, rather than personally?

For shareholders, the most consequential questions are whether sensitive information was compromised, whether regulatory violations occurred, whether the controversy affects Huang's ability to lead Nvidia, and whether it changes Nvidia's future earnings.

At present, public reporting does not establish that Nvidia lost valuable technology or that Huang knowingly participated in espionage.

That distinction is especially important when online discussion starts moving faster than verified information.

There is a genuine corporate investigation. There are allegations that remain unresolved. And there is a personal admission that, on its own, does not answer the national-security questions.

Investors should avoid treating those three things as interchangeable.

Nvidia stock was already under pressure before Sunday's announcement

Nvidia ended Friday, November 6, at $186.64, gaining 2.78% after Thursday's 9.26% fall.

However, Friday's recovery was less convincing than the closing gain might initially suggest.

Shares reached $194.90 during the session before retreating to $186.64, giving back most of the intraday advance from the opening price.

That suggests buyers were able to produce a rebound, but not retain much of it.

It does not prove further selling is inevitable. It does mean the stock has work to do before its recent decline looks convincingly repaired.

The weakness also needs broader market context. As investingLive reported in its review of the Nasdaq-100's November 5 selloff, selling extended across semiconductors, AI infrastructure and other major technology stocks.

It would therefore be misleading to attribute Nvidia's entire recent decline to the espionage reporting. The stock was already experiencing significant pressure from wider concerns about the AI investment cycle.

The November 6 closing price also predates Sunday's board announcement. It should not be mistaken for the market's response to that new development.

The Nvidia price map: What shareholders should watch if selling resumes

For existing holders, the question is not simply how far Nvidia could fall.

It is how the stock behaves at important prices and whether that behavior changes the evidence supporting a decision to hold, reduce exposure or consider buying.

A useful distinction is between three different outcomes.

A stock can test a level and hold, suggesting buyers are willing to defend it.

It can briefly break a level and recover, suggesting sellers have failed to maintain control.

Or it can break below a level and fail to recover it, a more concerning development because the previous support may now be acting as resistance.

That distinction is central to the following map.

$185-$187: The first stabilization test

This area surrounds Friday's $186.64 closing price.

If NVDA holds around this region and begins forming higher lows, it would improve the case that the stock is stabilizing.

If it quickly loses the area, particularly after an unsuccessful attempt to recover, attention shifts toward the November 5 low.

This is an early reference point, not a decisive verdict on the longer-term investment case.

$181.46: The first major downside decision

The November 5 low at $181.46 is especially important.

If Nvidia briefly moves beneath it but recovers and sustains trading back above the level, shareholders would have evidence that the attempted breakdown failed.

If the stock breaks below $181.46, remains there and subsequently struggles to reclaim it, the bearish scenario becomes more credible.

In that case, the first lower area to investigate is approximately $177-$180.

The important point is that a break followed by failed recovery is materially different from a temporary dip below support.

For a shareholder who has already decided their Nvidia exposure is too large, this distinction could help inform when to consider reducing risk.

$171-$173: The deeper support zone worth preparing for

If selling extends beyond $181.46 and $177-$180 cannot provide lasting support, my next priority is the $171-$173 region.

That area has historical relevance. Nvidia traded into the low $170s during March 2026, including a session low near $171 on March 26.

At Friday's closing price of $186.64, a move toward $172 would represent approximately another 7.8% decline.

That is a meaningful additional drawdown for someone already holding a large position.

But $172 should not be treated as a guaranteed buying opportunity.

What would interest me is whether the stock reaches the area, stops making lower lows, recovers above it and then successfully defends that recovery when sellers try again.

Conversely, a break below the zone followed by an unsuccessful rebound would increase the relevance of the next downside area.

$164-$165: A major historical reference

This is one of the more consequential areas on the map.

On March 30, 2026, Nvidia fell to approximately $164 before rebounding the following session. That makes $164-$165 an identifiable previous-low neighborhood.

At $164, NVDA would be approximately 12.1% beneath Friday's closing price.

Previous lows sometimes attract buyers because investors remember where a stock recovered before. But that memory is not a guarantee of support.

If shares revisit $164-$165, I would be looking for evidence that selling is losing effectiveness and buyers can retain a recovery.

If Nvidia instead breaks through the area and repeatedly fails to regain it, that would be a more important warning about the stock's broader price structure.

NVIDIA's $182 Lifeline: Will the Next Stop Be $164?

NVIDIA (NVDA) is testing a critical level on its monthly chart after a sharp retreat from September's $234.76 high.

November's decline has already pushed the stock to $181.46, briefly penetrating its rising 20-month EMA near $182.05.

The big question: Can NVIDIA defend this long-term trend indicator, or is the March low at $164.27 the next major downside target?

A sustained breakdown below $182 would increase the risk of a move toward $164, while a recovery above the EMA could suggest buyers are defending the longer-term bullish trend.

One important distinction: November's monthly candle is still developing. Testing the EMA is not the same as confirming a monthly breakdown.

$159.50-$160: The lower contingency

A decisive loss of $164-$165 would bring $159.50-$160 into focus as a deeper research watch area.

The $160 round number may attract attention, but it is not a verified historical floor, and this analysis does not forecast that Nvidia must reach it.

Only if that area also fails would the more distant $151-$154 contingency become relevant.

These lower zones are included to help shareholders consider the consequences of a prolonged decline, not to suggest such a decline is inevitable.

What if Nvidia rebounds instead?

A major error would be to assume that a bearish near-term price structure means Nvidia can only continue falling.

After significant declines, stocks can produce sharp recoveries. Some develop into lasting reversals; others provide temporary relief before selling resumes.

For Nvidia, there are two overhead areas worth distinguishing.

$194.90-$196.25: A recovery that still needs to prove itself

This zone incorporates the recent Friday and Thursday highs.

If Nvidia rallies toward it but stalls, reverses and subsequently fails to hold a higher low, the recovery would remain questionable.

For shareholders already uncomfortable with their allocation, such a rebound could offer an opportunity to reconsider position size without necessarily selling into the initial panic.

However, that is not the only interpretation.

If buyers break through the zone and retain it, the immediate bearish structure begins to improve.

The key is not simply reaching resistance, but what happens after the stock gets there.

$199.70-$200.15: A more meaningful recovery

The next major recovery area sits around $200, close to Nvidia's November 4 trading range.

A sustained advance through $194.90-$196.25, followed by successful retests and a recovery through approximately $199.70-$200.15, would represent more convincing technical improvement.

It would suggest buyers have repaired an important portion of the recent damage.

That would not guarantee a return to previous highs or remove the risks surrounding earnings and the investigation.

But it would make the immediate bearish scenario less persuasive.

A good analysis needs to identify what would prove its bearish interpretation wrong, not just where the stock might fall next.

Should Nvidia shareholders panic-sell?

A sharp price decline is a reason to reassess risk. It is not, by itself, a complete investment decision.

I would distinguish between three types of shareholders.

1. The long-term Nvidia investor with a manageable position

If the company's long-term competitive position, expected earnings and investment thesis remain attractive, short-term volatility does not automatically justify selling.

However, the investor should determine whether any new findings materially change the governance, regulatory or business outlook.

A price map can provide useful information without becoming the sole reason to exit a multi-year investment.

2. The shareholder with an oversized position

For someone whose portfolio is heavily concentrated in Nvidia, the issue can be different.

Even a company with strong financial performance can be an unsuitable concentration if another substantial decline would create financial or emotional pressure.

Such a shareholder might consider reducing part of the exposure, whether after a failed recovery near $195, following a sustained breakdown under $181.46, or simply because their allocation exceeds their intended risk limit.

Selling part of a position does not necessarily mean abandoning the investment thesis.

It may mean preserving some upside participation while reducing the damage another decline could cause.

3. The investor considering buying more Nvidia

Lower prices can improve an investment's prospective return, provided the underlying business outlook has not deteriorated enough to offset that improvement.

But there is a difference between a stock becoming cheaper and a stock becoming attractive.

A fall toward $172 or $164 could make Nvidia worth investigating more closely. It would not be sufficient evidence on its own to buy.

A successful recovery above an important area, improving price behavior and a business outlook that still supports the valuation would make the decision better informed.

An investor may also choose to wait until after the next earnings report or until the independent investigation offers more clarity.

There is no obligation to buy simply because the price has declined.

Nvidia earnings on November 17 add another layer of risk

Nvidia is scheduled to report fiscal third-quarter 2027 results on Tuesday, November 17, with results expected after the US regular trading session and its conference call scheduled for 5 p.m. ET.

This means investors face two distinct uncertainties.

The investigation may produce more information about governance and national-security concerns.

Meanwhile, earnings will test the strength of Nvidia's business, including AI infrastructure demand, margins, guidance and the sustainability of its growth expectations.

A strong earnings report could help restore confidence. Weak guidance or disappointing business developments could deepen existing selling pressure, regardless of the eventual outcome of the investigation.

Shareholders should also remember that stocks can gap sharply after earnings. A technical watch level cannot guarantee that an order will execute at that price.

For further practical context, see investingLive's guide to managing stock exposure ahead of earnings.

What to watch when Nvidia trading resumes Monday

Nasdaq-100 futures are scheduled to reopen Sunday evening at 6 p.m. ET. They can offer an early indication of wider technology-market sentiment, although they do not establish where Nvidia itself will trade.

On Monday, November 9, the first direct indications should come from NVDA's premarket trading, beginning at 4 a.m. ET on Nasdaq.

Premarket prices can move disproportionately when liquidity is limited, so a fleeting move through a watch level should be treated cautiously.

Once regular trading begins at 9:30 a.m. ET, the more useful questions are whether Nvidia holds its opening range, whether rallies are sustained and whether the stock is outperforming or underperforming the wider Nasdaq market.

A particularly weak Nvidia performance while the Nasdaq recovers would suggest company-specific selling pressure deserves greater attention.

Conversely, a comparatively resilient Nvidia share price despite continued index weakness could be an encouraging early sign, although not definitive evidence of a bottom.

Investors can also monitor Nvidia's response to the congressional briefing request, for which lawmakers asked for a reply by November 11. The requested briefing date is November 18.

Nvidia stock outlook: Prepare for evidence, not headlines alone

Nvidia shareholders have legitimate reasons to take this controversy seriously.

The company's board has launched an investigation, US lawmakers are asking questions, and the national-security issues raised by the reporting are consequential.

But it is equally important not to treat allegations as established findings.

From a stock-price perspective, $181.46 is the immediate downside test, $171-$173 is the important deeper decision zone, and $164-$165 is the historical-low neighborhood. A sustained recovery through approximately $195-$200 would weaken the immediate bearish scenario.

For the investor facing the difficult choice between selling, holding, trimming or buying more, the most useful approach may be to establish in advance which developments would change that decision.

That includes both the evidence emerging from the investigation and what Nvidia's price actually does.

There is a substantial difference between reacting to a frightening headline and responding to new information that changes the risks of owning a stock.

This analysis is educational and is not personalized investment advice. Market levels are conditional references, not forecasts or guaranteed execution prices. Investors should consider their financial circumstances, portfolio concentration and risk tolerance before making decisions.

This article was written by Itai Levitan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Rubio says Iran talks not productive as Tehran’s demands are unacceptable
item.description:
For oil, this is the more important signal of the weekend. Trump made avoiding renewed strikes conditional on progress in talks, and his Secretary of State now says there isn’t any. That pushes escalation risk back toward the front of the market’s mind and argues for a firmer war-risk premium in crude. Combined with the suspected Iranian strike on Iraq’s Khor Mor gas field, the de-escalation story from Trump’s CNN interview looks shakier. Traders are likely to be more cautious about selling crude on hopes of a deal. Any fresh threat to US forces or to Hormuz shipping would test Rubio’s pledge to respond.

Trump set progress in talks as the condition for holding off on new strikes, and his top diplomat is now saying that condition isn’t being met, a shift that puts escalation risk firmly back in the frame.

Summary:

  • Rubio said negotiations with Iran are not productive because Tehran’s demands are simply unacceptable.
  • He said a diplomatic solution is sometimes not possible, though the US will keep exploring whether one exists.
  • The US is taking defensive action and will respond if its forces in the region are threatened.
  • Rubio stressed long-standing cross-party agreement that a nuclear-armed Iran would be completely unacceptable.
  • The tone contrasts with Trump’s weekend comments that renewed strikes were highly unlikely if talks progressed.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has said negotiations with Iran are not productive because Tehran’s demands are simply unacceptable. It is a noticeably harder tone than President Donald Trump took shortly before, and it raises fresh doubts over the prospects for a deal to end the war.

Rubio said a diplomatic solution is sometimes not possible, although Washington would continue to explore whether a chance for one exists. He added that the US is taking defensive action and will respond if its forces in the region are threatened.

He also stressed long-standing agreement across both major US political parties that Iran acquiring nuclear weapons would be completely unacceptable and would pose a serious threat to US security. The remark appears aimed at signalling that Washington’s core red line will not shift, whatever the political pressures at home after last week’s midterm elections.

The comments contrast with Trump’s message over the weekend. He said renewed US military action against Iran was highly unlikely as long as talks over Tehran’s nuclear programme and the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz showed progress. Rubio’s assessment that the talks are not making headway goes to the heart of that condition. If progress is the test for avoiding further strikes, the top US diplomat is now saying it is not being met.

The shift also comes against a backdrop of rising regional tension. A suspected Iranian drone strike on Sunday halted production at Iraq’s Khor Mor gas field and knocked out a large share of the Kurdistan region’s power supply, while the US has been tightening economic pressure on Tehran.

Eight months into the conflict, the two sides remain at a stalemate, with Iranian attacks on tankers transiting Hormuz continuing. The next signals to watch are whether Washington sets a timeline for the talks, any change in US force posture in the region, and whether Tehran hardens or softens its own position. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

Final official results from the Electoral Commission are due on November 27, and coalition negotiations could take weeks after that. Labour leader Chris Hipkins did not concede, insisting that every vote must be counted.

National’s share of the vote fell to around 29% from about 38% in 2023. Hours after Trump said renewed US strikes on Iran were unlikely, a suspected Iranian drone knocked out most of Kurdistan’s power supply, a reminder that the region’s energy infrastructure remains a live target whatever the diplomatic mood.

Summary:

  • A drone strike on Sunday evening hit a gas storage facility at Iraq’s Khor Mor gas field, halting production.
  • The Kurdistan region lost nearly 2.8 gigawatts of generation, roughly two thirds of its normal power supply.
  • No group has claimed responsibility. Iran or its allied Iraqi militias are suspected.
  • The attack came hours after Trump said renewed US military action against Iran was highly unlikely if talks progress.
  • The field supplies regional power generation rather than exports, so the direct global supply impact is limited.
  • Washington is separately pressing Iraq to close all but two border crossings with Iran.

A suspected Iranian drone strike has halted production at Iraq’s Khor Mor gas field, one of the largest in the Kurdistan region. It knocked out nearly 2.8 gigawatts of power generation in what appears to be a significant escalation in the regional fallout from the Iran war.

Two security sources told Reuters that a drone targeted the field on Sunday evening, with smoke seen rising from the site in Chamchamal, Sulaymaniyah province. An engineer at the field said a gas storage facility was hit, and all crew were ordered into shelters for fear of further attacks.

The Kurdistan region’s electricity ministry said nearly 2.8 gigawatts of generating capacity was lost from the grid. With the region normally producing around 4 gigawatts, that implies roughly two thirds of its power supply was taken offline, leaving households and businesses facing outages.

No group has claimed responsibility. Suspicion has fallen on Iran or its allied militias in Iraq, which have carried out repeated missile and drone attacks on the Kurdistan region since the war began. Kurdish authorities have long blamed Iran-backed armed groups for strikes on Khor Mor. The field has been hit many times in recent years, including an attack in November last year that also halted production.

The timing stands out. The strike came only hours after US President Donald Trump said renewed US military action against Iran was highly unlikely as long as talks over Tehran’s nuclear programme and the Strait of Hormuz made progress. If Iranian involvement is confirmed, the attack would suggest that Tehran or its proxies are still prepared to hit regional energy infrastructure even as diplomatic contacts pick up.

Khor Mor is operated by Pearl Petroleum, a consortium that includes UAE-based Dana Gas and Crescent Petroleum. Its gas feeds power plants in the Kurdistan region rather than export markets, so the direct effect on global supply is limited.

Pressure on Iraq is also building from Washington. Iraq’s foreign minister said the US Treasury has asked Baghdad to close all but two of its border crossings with Iran, as part of a wider push to tighten economic pressure on Tehran.

Attention now turns to how quickly production can be restored, whether responsibility is formally assigned, and how Washington responds to an attack that cuts across its message of restraint.

item.description:
For oil, Trump’s comments trim the risk that the US resumes strikes, which could take some of the war-risk premium out of crude. Trump is signalling that he would rather settle than strike, but with carriers in position, sanctions tightening and Hormuz still contested, the burden is on Tehran to deliver progress before the military option comes back into play.

Summary:

  • Trump said renewed US military action against Iran is “highly unlikely” as long as talks on Tehran’s nuclear programme and reopening the Strait of Hormuz make progress.
  • He said three US aircraft carriers are in the region and that infrastructure targets, including power plants and bridges, have been identified, though he would prefer not to hit them.
  • Trump claimed Iran’s air defences are destroyed and that it retains only about 10% of its missile capacity and 15% of its drone capability.
  • The war is in an eight-month stalemate, with Iranian attacks on tankers in Hormuz and little visible diplomatic progress.
  • Washington is adding pressure: a reward of up to $20 million for nuclear programme information and a task force to block land transfers of weapons.
  • Diplomatic contacts have increased since the US midterms, including a Trump call with Qatar’s emir on de-escalation.

US President Donald Trump has said it is “highly unlikely” he will need to order renewed military action against Iran, provided negotiations over Tehran’s nuclear programme and the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz show progress. He repeated the point five times during a roughly 20-minute phone interview with CNN on Sunday.

Trump tied the outcome to whether Iran signs what he called a very strong agreement, while stressing that he would act if necessary. He argued that Tehran is under severe economic strain, claiming its inflation rate had reached around 300% this year, and said US strikes had already hit the country hard. In his view, Iran is keen to reach a deal.

He also made clear that US forces remain in position. Trump said three aircraft carriers are now in the region, with the latest having just arrived. He said the US has identified infrastructure targets, including power plants and dozens of bridges that he said could be brought down within an hour. He added that he would prefer not to destroy that infrastructure, given how long it would take to rebuild.

On Iran’s defensive capacity, Trump claimed its air defences had been destroyed. He also claimed the regime retains only around 10% of its missile capacity and 15% of its drone capability, as many of its factories have been knocked out. These figures have not been independently verified.

Eight months into the war, the two sides have been locked in a stalemate, with little military action or diplomatic progress, even as tankers transiting Hormuz have come under Iranian attack. Qatar, which has mediated the talks, has said little publicly about their status. Iranian hardliners have taken last week’s US midterm results, which reflected the war’s unpopularity with American voters, as a sign that Washington may be more willing to accept Tehran’s demands on its nuclear programme and control of the strait.

At the same time, Washington appears to be adding pressure rather than easing it. The US military is offering a reward of up to $20 million for information on Iran’s nuclear programme. It has also set up a task force to stop Tehran moving advanced weapons and materials over land. Iran continues to struggle to sell crude under US sanctions, with billions of dollars in overseas assets frozen.

Diplomatic contacts have picked up since the midterms. Qatar said on Friday that Trump had called Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani to discuss de-escalation. That came a day after Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi spoke with counterparts across the Gulf and the wider region.

The next test is whether that flurry of calls turns into visible movement at the negotiating table, or whether the stalemate in Hormuz drags on.
